(Chris Sweda/Chicago Tribune) Expand By Brad Biggs | bmbiggs@chicagotribune.com | Chicago Tribune PUBLISHED: November 8, 2026 at 6:00 AM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... As an undrafted free agent who entered the league in 2016 out of Holy Cross with a signing bonus of $2,000, Kalif Raymond knows what it’s like to have an NFL dream squashed.
 He knows the clues signaling bad news. They become familiar when you’ve been cut nine times. So he also knows the challenges in reinventing himself to find a little edge and maybe become a little more marketable for the next team.
 “All of them are pretty, pretty rough,” Raymond said. “When you get a phone call and it’s from the team and you don’t have the number saved, you get very nervous.”
 Fortunately for Raymond, it has been some time since he has been on the receiving end of one of those calls informing him a transaction is about to happen. He has established himself as a dangerous punt returner and shifty wide receiver and, maybe more importantly, as a player who’s more valuable to teammates than he is to coaches.
 Inside Caleb Williams’ blooming connection with his Big 3: Colston Loveland, Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III 
 Raymond began the season on a tear. He caught a career-high eight passes for 84 yards in the Week 1 road victory against the Carolina Panthers . After three games, he led the team with 19 receptions for 214 yards. In a high-powered passing attack that was supposed to feature tight end Colston Loveland and wide receivers Luther Burden III and Rome Odunze, Raymond was the guy making the most plays.
 Predictably, the other three have gotten increased volume, especially since Caleb Williams returned from a hamstring injury on Oct. 18 in Atlanta. Raymond has settled into the No. 3 role he was signed to fill in free agency. Still, entering Sunday night’s game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the 32-year-old veteran in his 11th season is on pace for a career year.
 Raymond has 28 receptions for 258 yards and one touchdown and needs just 20 more catches to match his career high from 2021, the season Ben Johnson was the passing game coordinator for the Detroit Lions.
 He’s a sparkplug capable of making big plays too. On Monday night, a comfortable 11-point lead had shrunk to 20-17 midway through the fourth quarter. Facing a tense third-and-9 at the Seahawks 44-yard line, Williams lateraled to Raymond on a designed screen. Raymond darted 39 yards on the play — which officially counted as a run — to set up D’Andre Swift’s game-sealing touchdown. It was the offense’s biggest play of the night, and it buried the Seahawks.
 Raymond also has been incredibly friendly to the quarterbacks. His catch percentage of 82.4% (28 receptions on 34 targets) is the highest among all NFL receivers with a minimum of 25 targets. He has a knack for getting open, finding soft spots in coverage over the middle, and his hands are sure.
 He makes certain of that. Raymond is the last player off the practice field nearly every day. On Thursday, he exited 40 minutes after practice ended. He catches 205 passes from the Jugs machine after practice. Every day.
 Bears wide receiver Kalif Raymond (14) waits in the tunnel with teammates before a game against the Falcons on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, in Atlanta. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) 
 Why 205?
 “Because Amon-Ra St. Brown catches 202, and I am trying to beat him and he is a two-time All-Pro,” Raymond said. “I have no excuse not to be catching 205 at this point.”
 Raymond also takes extra reps on routes if his timing feels off or the ball doesn’t come his way during practice.
 “I don’t want my first time seeing it to be during the game,” he said.
 After Raymond signed with the Bears in free agency, St. Brown referred to him as the “greatest teammate I’ve ever had” on “The St. Brown Podcast.” When asked how Raymond earned that lofty praise, St. Brown spoke for nearly five minutes about the the person, not the player.
 “‘Lif would do whatever it takes for the team,” St. Brown said. “He is very supportive of his teammates. Obviously you want that in a teammate, but I think ‘Lif supports teammates in all ways not just on the field. He’s shown up to so many things I’ve had outside of football, just randomly would be there to show support.
 “He’s one of the nicest guys ever. Super unselfish. Ask the people that work in equipment or PR or anything outside of the coaches in the building and they will all tell you he is one of the nicest guys. He’s just an all-around great dude.”
 5 things to watch in Chicago Bears-Tampa Bay Buccaneers matchup on Sunday night — plus our Week 9 predictions 
 Raymond and St. Brown arrived in Detroit in 2021. Raymond had caught 20 passes to that point in his NFL career, a fringe free-agent addition who had competition for a role from St. Brown, a fourth-round pick out of USC.
 “When I got here he was asking me a lot of questions about where I am from,” St. Brown said. “That’s what makes him such a great teammate — he gets to know his teammates. He’s always asking questions about you rather than talking about himself.”
 Told how St. Brown called Raymond the greatest teammate, Tyson Bagent nodded affirmingly.
 “I can see that,” Bagent said.
 Then the backup quarterback detailed how Raymond met him for a throwing session in June in Shepherdstown, W.Va., about 10 miles from Bagent’s hometown of Martinsburg.
 “We had some pretty high-level throwing sessions,” Bagent said. “He came and just jumped right in like he’s one of the guys. He was coaching everyone up. He’s unbelievable. Answered every question any of my guys had. It was cool for them to see someone as fast and as crisp as him running around.
 “One of the nicest guys you will run into. Just a real charming, nice guy. He makes you feel good about yourself. Very positive and he’s a small-school super vet. You’d be really happy if your kid grew up to be like Kalif Raymond.”
 Second-year receiver Jahdae Walker said Raymond’s voice in the room helps
 because he’ll ask questions that might be difficyult for first- or second-year players to form.
 “He’s a leader, cool in the locker room, you can bond with him,” Walker said. “There is so much I can say about Kalif in a good way.”
 Bears wide receiver Kalif Raymond (14) is tackled by Seahawks cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett after a long run in the fourth quarter at Lumen Field on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in Seattle. (Chris Sweda/Chicago Tribune) 
 Raymond got 48 of 70 snaps in the victory over the Seahawks, six more than Burden. Playing time for the skill-position players is always game-plan dependent, but the only receiver with more snaps through eight games is Odunze. That’s in large part because the smallest player on the roster who isn’t kicker Cairo Santos — Raymond is 5-foot-8 and 180 pounds — blocks like a much bigger man.

 Raymond is fearless as blocker, not just attacking defensive backs downfield but happy to throw his weight at defensive ends and linebackers near the line of scrimmage. That tenacity, bundled with the energy he brings to everything he does, quickly made him a favorite.
 “Such a positive dude and mindset,” Loveland said. “It damn sure spreads.”
 The positive energy Raymond radiates was needed in 2018. He split the 2017 season in New York between the Jets and Giants, and when he walked off the field at the end of the year, he thought his career might be over.
 He found a niche in Tennessee in 2019, and when he landed in Detroit — where Johnson was — things started to click. Brought in on a one-year, $3.5 million contract, Raymond has been exactly what the coach expected. Johnson advocated for his signing in free agency, knowing Raymond’s veteran presence would be a perfect fit for an offense with so much youth.”
 “I think they all feed off him,” Johnson said. “We’ve got guys in every position room right now that are, they’re really the epitome of what you want it to look like, and he leads that charge.
 “Selfless player, hardest worker. I can’t say enough good things about him and his impact, whether they’re production-based or not. He elevates everybody on the offense, in the receiver room and really on the team as well.”
 Scouting report
 Buccaneers linebacker Josiah Trotter, right, pressures Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. during the second half at Raymond James Stadium on Nov. 1, 2026, in Tampa, Fla. (Mike Carlson/Getty) 
 Josiah Trotter, Buccaneers middle linebacker 
 Information for this report was obtained from NFL scouts. 
 Trotter, 6-foot-2 and 237 pounds, is a rookie the Bucs selected in the second round at No. 46 in their bid to replace mainstay Lavonte David. The son of Jeremiah Trotter, a four-time Pro Bowl selection for the Philadelphia Eagles, Josiah split his college career between West Virginia and Missouri.
 Trotter ranks third among rookies with 62 tackles and has a pick-six against the Cincinnati Bengals’ Joe Burrow along with one sack and three pass breakups.
 “Josiah Trotter has outstanding play recognition,” the scout said. “Looks like he’s a step ahead at times when you watch him. When the guard pulls, he’s there. He takes a downhill, physical angle and he’s violent at the point of attack. He’s a very good tackler. Good lateral change-of-direction ability to slip past blockers, and when he tackles, he thumps you. He’s a wrap-you-up-and-run-his-feet tackler. He’s better in coverage than I thought he would be. He’s not an elite coverage linebacker, but Todd Bowles helps him out because they do so much disguising at the line of scrimmage that he’ll be mugged up at the A gap and then drop out and fall into the passing lane. He’ll put him in position where the ball is going to be thrown at times.
 “He’s getting better in terms of getting to depth and playing with his eyes and driving on the football. He’s never going to be Fred Warner in coverage, but that’s OK because this system maximizes what he can do. And he’s a really good blizter. Those linebackers blitz a lot for the Buccaneers. They do a lot with them, and I’d expect to see a lot of that Sunday night. They have to try to create disruption.”
